exercise1.prompt: Indexing and Slicing Arrays: Everything but the ends

hiddenCases.name: three items leave one in the middle

exercise1.hint: A slice from 1 to -1 drops one from each end, and slices clamp rather than raise when there is nothing left to take.

exercise2.prompt: Indexing and Slicing Arrays: Zero a range without touching the original

hiddenCases.name: the whole array can be zeroed

exercise2.hint: Take a .copy() first, then assign 0 into the slice of the copy. Assigning into a slice of the original would change the caller's array, which is the thing this exercise is checking.

questions.prompt: How does slicing an array differ from slicing a list?
choices: The array slice is a view, so writing to it changes the original
The array slice is always shorter
questions.explain: No copy is made. This is efficient and it is also the source of a whole class of accidental edits.
"Every row, column 1" — which is how you take a column out of a two-dimensional array in one expression.

questions.prompt: How do you take a slice you can safely modify?
questions.explain: copy() makes the new block of memory that a list slice would have given you anyway.

questions.prompt: a = np.array([1,2,3,4]); a[1:3] = 0. What is a?
questions.explain: Assigning a single number into a slice broadcasts it across every position in that slice.
